title: String Matching: KMP Search
oneLiner: Find every occurrence of a pattern in O(n + m) by precomputing, for each prefix of the pattern, how much of it can be reused after a mismatch.
keyTakeaway: When a match fails after j characters, those j characters of text are already known: they equal pattern[0..j-1]. KMP precomputes lps[j-1], the longest proper prefix of that piece which is also a suffix of it, and jumps j straight there without moving back in the text. The text pointer only moves forward, so the search is O(n) after an O(m) precomputation.
explanation:
Given a text and a non-empty pattern, return every index where the pattern starts in the text, in increasing order. Matches may overlap: "aa" occurs in "aaaaa" at 0, 1, 2 and 3. The goal is O(n + m) for a text of length n and a pattern of length m.

The naive search tries every start position and compares up to m characters there, so it's O(n·m) in the worst case. Search for "aaaa...ab" (1,000 a's then a b) in a text of 2,000 a's and a b: at almost every start, the naive loop matches 1,000 a's, fails on the b, then moves the start forward by one and compares nearly the same 1,000 a's again. All that rework is information it already had.

KMP keeps that information. Define the prefix function, also called the failure function or lps (longest proper prefix that is also a suffix): lps[i] is the length of the longest string that is both a proper prefix and a suffix of pattern[0..i]. For "abab" it's [0, 0, 1, 2]: "abab" ends with "ab", which is also how it starts. Now scan the text with j = the number of pattern characters currently matched. If text[i] == pattern[j], j++. If they differ and j > 0, set j = lps[j - 1] and compare text[i] again: the last lps[j - 1] matched characters are already a prefix of the pattern, so you continue from there instead of starting over. If j == 0 and they differ, just move i on. When j reaches m, record a match at i - m + 1, then set j = lps[m - 1] so overlapping matches are found.

Building lps is the same algorithm run on the pattern against itself: keep length = lps[i - 1]; while pattern[i] != pattern[length] and length > 0, fall back with length = lps[length - 1]; if they match, length++; then lps[i] = length. Each fallback undoes at least one earlier increment, so both loops are linear overall: O(m) to build, O(n) to search, O(m) extra space.

In practice, library calls like IndexOf and str.find are fine for a single lookup. KMP matters when you need a worst-case guarantee, all occurrences, or the prefix function itself: it also answers "shortest period of a string" (m - lps[m - 1]), "longest prefix that is also a suffix", and "shortest palindrome by adding characters in front". Rabin-Karp (rolling hash) is the other standard linear-time approach; it's simpler to extend to many patterns but needs a collision check.

The visualization first builds lps for "abab", then searches "abacababab", where one mismatch falls back twice and two matches overlap.

visualizationSteps.message: Step 1: build lps for the pattern "abab". lps[0] is always 0: a single character has no proper prefix that is also a suffix.
"ab": no proper prefix is also a suffix, so lps[1] = 0.
"aba" starts and ends with "a", so lps[2] = 1.
"abab" starts and ends with "ab", so lps[3] = 2.
Step 2: scan the text "abacababab" with lps = [0, 0, 1, 2]. j counts how many pattern characters currently match. The text pointer never moves back.
i = 3 ('c'): 'c' != pattern[3] = 'b', fall back j = lps[2] = 1; 'c' != pattern[1] = 'b', fall back j = lps[0] = 0; 'c' != pattern[0] either, j stays 0 and i moves on.
i = 7 ('b'): matches pattern[3], j = 4; full match at 4, so record it and set j = lps[3] = 2 to keep overlaps.
i = 9 ('b'): matches pattern[3], j = 4; full match at 6, so record it and set j = lps[3] = 2 to keep overlaps.
Done: [4, 6]. The text pointer only moved forward: the mismatch at the c fell back through lps instead of restarting, and the overlapping match came from j = lps[3] after the first one.

recognitionSignals: Find a pattern (or all of its occurrences) in a long text with a guaranteed linear bound, especially with repetitive inputs like "aaaa...ab".
Questions about a string's borders: its period, its longest prefix that is also a suffix, or whether it is a repetition of a smaller block.
You notice a naive matcher re-reading text it has already compared after every mismatch.
gotchas: On a mismatch, don't advance the text pointer: fall back with j = lps[j - 1] and compare the SAME text character again, possibly several times.
After a full match, set j = lps[m - 1], not 0. Resetting to 0 misses overlapping matches like "abab" at index 2 in "abababab".
lps[i] is about pattern[0..i] inclusive and must be a PROPER prefix (shorter than the whole piece), so lps[0] is always 0 and the build loop starts at i = 1.
confusableWith: Naive search (try every start, compare up to m characters) gives the same answers and is what IndexOf-style loops do. It's O(n·m) in the worst case, which repetitive inputs expose.

Rabin-Karp compares rolling hashes of each length-m window instead, also O(n + m) on average. It extends easily to many patterns at once but must verify on a hash match, and a bad hash degrades it to O(n·m).

complexity.note: Building lps is O(m) and the scan is O(n): each fallback undoes an earlier increment of j, and the text pointer never moves back. lps has one entry per pattern character (the list of matches can add up to n more).
